title: Can you be gormful, wistless or ert? | LOST POSITIVES

entries.note: A word rarely found without its prefix or suffix, such as [[see:disgusted]], whose base form should exist under English word-building rules but doesn't.
Arrived in the late 16th century from French desgouster, to dislike the taste, ultimately from Latin [[from:gustare]], to taste; it has no natural opposite.
The missing opposite of [[see:disgusted]]; a word gust, from Latin [[from:gustare]], would simply mean taste.
Old English word meaning to cover over, overthrow or submerge completely, like a ship in rough water; often used jokingly to mean merely okay.
A hyperbolic form of [[from:whelm]], keeping its sense of being completely submerged.
Coined later as a playful twist and opposite of [[see:overwhelmed]], though underwhelming a boat would also sound like drowning it.
The dis- intensifies rather than negates, as in [[see:distribute]]; gruntle means to grunt, so it is to be grumbly like an irritated pig.
Only in the dictionary because [[see:P. G. Wodehouse]] used it jokingly in The Code of the Woosters as the opposite of [[see:disgruntled]].
Author, adored by Rob, whose Code of the Woosters gives the earliest citation of [[see:gruntled]].
Example of dis- meaning widely rather than negating, cited to explain [[see:disgruntled]].
Like the dis- in [[see:disgruntled]], the off intensifies the annoyance instead of negating it.
Via French chaloir, to matter, from Latin [[from:calere]], to be hot; not hot-headed. Possibly invented by the English, as earliest citations are English.
The nonexistent opposite of [[see:nonchalant]], which would mean worked up, hot-tempered or intensely interested.
A short-lived English word meaning warm or hot, taken more directly from Latin [[from:calere]], source of [[same-root:nonchalant]].
From Latin [[from:non plus]], no more: so surprised you have nothing more to say or do; often taken to mean unimpressed.
The forgotten opposite of [[see:innocent]], meaning knowing or guilty, quoted from a 1685 letter to James II; [[see:guilty]] won out.
The word that won out in English over [[see:nocent]] as the opposite of [[see:innocent]].
Literally unknowing, so it can mean pure or naive; Susie Dent called [[see:nocent]] a lost negative, but Jess argues innocent can be pejorative.
Rob's term for a word like [[see:nocent]] whose un-negated form has disappeared; Susie Dent corrected him to [[see:lost negative]].
Susie Dent's label for [[see:nocent]], since being nocent is a bad thing.
From Latin, unstained: unsullied and untarnished; Susie Dent's further example of a word with a lost opposite.
The missing opposite of [[see:immaculate]], meaning stained.
Eye condition where eyesight becomes stained or foggy, showing the stain root of [[same-root:immaculate]].
Shares its stain root with [[same-root:immaculate]]; Rob noticed it in a coffee shop.
Milk stained with a little coffee, from [[from:macchiato]].
Also caffè macchiato: coffee stained with a little frothy milk, from [[from:macchiato]].
From the 14th century: beyond expression due to greatness, as in God's ineffable wisdom; literally unable to be spoken.
The hypothetical opposite of [[see:ineffable]], something able to be said aloud; Rob thinks it sounds saucy.
Means useless; feck is essentially the same word as [[same-root:effect]], having split off from it.
Once existed, meaning effective or efficacious, quoted from 1568: the lost opposite of [[see:feckless]].
Basically the same word as the feck in [[same-root:feckless]].
Describes someone who regrets nothing, however brutal; its opposite survives as [[see:rueful]] rather than ruthful.
To bitterly regret, as in you'll rue the day; the older word, from Old English.
Noun form of [[see:rue]], from Old Norse, gaining its -th on the model of [[see:truth]] and [[see:growth]]; it meant something like mercy.
The existing opposite of [[see:ruthless]], used instead of ruthful.
With true, a model for forming [[see:ruth]] from [[see:rue]].
With grow, a model for forming [[see:ruth]] from [[see:rue]].
The given name comes from a Hebrew word for friendship, [[unrelated:ruth]] meaning mercy, though Rob thinks Ruths should enjoy the double meaning.
Means unaware or inattentive, from [[from:gorm]]; gormful has never existed in English.
Never an English word, though it would be the opposite of [[see:gormless]].
From the Vikings' Old Norse; to take gorm was to pay attention or heed.
Built on [[from:wist]]; it came to mean bittersweet melancholy or nostalgia through [[from:had-I-wist]].
An archaic term meaning to know, existing in a different form in Old English.
Middle and early modern English noun for regret over a rash action, as in had-I-wist cometh too late; compared to [[see:hindsight is 20/20]].
A modern parallel to [[see:had-I-wist]].
Borrowed from French, meaning unavoidable; English has lost its positive [[see:evitable]].
A former English word meaning avoidable, the opposite of [[see:inevitable]].
Looked up live: from Latin [[from:vadere]], to go, with e- meaning out, so to go away from; [[unrelated:evitable]].
Differs from tax avoidance because [[see:evade]] and [[see:evitable]] have different roots.
From Latin exasperare, to roughen thoroughly, from [[from:asper]], rough, with intensifying ex-; it grates like sandpaper; [[unrelated:aspirate]].
Sounds like it relates to breathing and looks like an opposite of [[unrelated:exasperate]], but isn't one.
Means hardship, literally a rough patch in life; a relative of [[same-root:exasperate]].
From Latin [[from:aspergere]], to sprinkle, so to cast aspersions is to sprinkle negativity; [[unrelated:exasperate]].
Already discussed in an earlier episode, along with its folk name sparrow grass.
A lost variant of [[see:apt]], unused for centuries except as a humorous opposite of [[see:inept]], as in a 1966 Time Magazine quote.
Means the same as [[see:inapt]]: inappropriate for the situation.
Basically the same word as [[see:ept]].
Means the same as [[see:inept]]: inappropriate for the situation.
Something you're not good at, in contrast to [[see:ineptitude]].
Means being clumsy, in contrast to [[see:inaptitude]].
Meant powerless in the 14th century; by the 16th it meant clumsy, and now difficult to handle because of size, like a heavy sword.
An Old English word meaning active or vigorous that didn't survive, leaving only [[see:unwieldy]].
Rob wonders whether it is a word, and Jess approves it.
